cards.front: Row-oriented vs column-oriented storage: what does each pack together on disk?
cards.back: Row storage packs all columns of one row together (good for whole-row reads and inserts). Columnar storage packs all values of one column together (good for aggregates that touch few columns).

cards.front: Why do databases read data in large fixed-size pages (64 MB in nanoDB) instead of individual records?
cards.back: IO devices are slow, so bulk operations keep cost in check: one 64 MB read beats 2,000 separate 32 KB reads. Every table lives as a DbFile packed into these fixed pages.

cards.front: How does a slotted page organize variable-length rows?
cards.back: Rows pack from the top down, a slot array of (offset, length) pointers grows from the bottom up, and free space shrinks in the middle. Moving a grown row only repoints its slot, so external (page_id, slot_id) references stay stable.

cards.front: Why do columns compress much better than rows, especially at scale?
cards.back: A column is uniform in type and full of repetition (popular songs repeat, timestamps run nearly sequential), which encoders exploit — commonly 5:1 to 10:1 at hundreds of millions of rows. A row mixes types, which defeats most encoders. Repetition only emerges at scale.

cards.front: What is PAX, and which popular file format uses it?
cards.back: PAX is row-grouped columnar: slice rows into row-groups, then store each column contiguously inside the group. Parquet uses it — ~128 MB row-groups, per-column chunks, one file for the whole table.

cards.front: How does Parquet's footer let a query skip data without reading it?
cards.back: The footer stores per-row-group min/max statistics for each column. A query reads the footer first and skips the column data of any row-group whose min/max range cannot match the predicate.

cards.front: What are BigQuery's three pillars for scanning petabytes in seconds?
cards.back: 1) Columnar layout — read only the referenced columns; 2) Compression — dictionary and run-length encoding shrink the read another order of magnitude; 3) Distribution — the scan shards across thousands of on-demand workers in a tree.

cards.front: What system did Google's Dremel paper (2010) introduce, and what bottleneck did it fix?
cards.back: Dremel — shipped as BigQuery — introduced nested columnar storage with tree-based execution. It fixed the row-storage problem where querying one tiny field (e.g. Date) forced reading megabytes of HTML Body per record.

cards.front: What does "storage decoupled from compute" mean in BigQuery?
cards.back: Data lives in storage independently of query workers; thousands of leaf workers spin up only for the seconds a query runs, each scanning a slice of the needed columns, then disappear.

cards.front: How does hybrid storage serve 1M inserts/sec AND 100 ms analytics on one table?
cards.back: Fresh writes land in small row-oriented parts (fast whole-row appends); a background merge converts aged parts into compressed columnar segments (fast scans). Data age picks the layout automatically, and one query engine reads both.

cards.front: How does ClickHouse's MergeTree relate to LSM trees?
cards.back: MergeTree's "parts + background merging" is an LSM-tree variation. The twist: traditional LSM trees merge row-to-row, while ClickHouse merges row-shaped parts into columnar-compressed segments.

cards.front: What is the IO cost of one hash-partitioning pass over N pages, and why is that the whole point?
cards.back: 2N — read every page once, write every page once. That linear pass turns a RAM-blind O(N²) problem into RAM-sized partitions each processed once, making downstream sorts, joins, and group-bys linear.

cards.front: Which key property of hash partitioning makes per-partition processing correct?
cards.back: The same key always hashes to the same partition (hash(key) % B), so all of one user's rows land in one partition no matter when they appear — each partition can be processed independently without missing matches.

cards.front: What are BigSort's two phases?
cards.back: Phase 1 (divide): read RAM-sized chunks, quicksort each in memory, write them back as sorted runs. Phase 2 (conquer): repeatedly k-way merge the runs — B−1 input buffers plus 1 output buffer — until one sorted file remains.

cards.front: General IO cost of BigSort on N pages with B buffer pages?
cards.back: 2N × (1 + ⌈log_(B−1)(N/B)⌉): each pass reads and writes every page (2N), one pass builds runs, and each merge pass folds ~B−1 runs into one. The familiar 4N is just the single-merge-pass best case.

cards.front: What does replacement selection buy BigSort's Phase 1?
cards.back: Streaming input through a B-page in-memory heap grows runs to about 2B pages on average instead of B, roughly halving the run count to ⌈N/2B⌉ and potentially saving a whole merge pass. (This is the form the exam equations use.)

cards.front: Why is external sort called "the backbone of a database"?
cards.back: Every ORDER BY, every B+Tree range scan, every sort-merge join, and every LSM compaction is built on it. PostgreSQL, BigQuery, and Spark all run the same operation underneath.

cards.front: IO cost formula for Block Nested Loop Join of R (outer) and S (inner) with B buffer pages?
cards.back: P(R) + ⌈P(R)/B⌉ × P(S) + OUT: read R once in blocks, and re-scan all of S once per R-block. Best case (R fits in B pages): P(R) + P(S) + OUT.

cards.front: In BNLJ, which table goes on the outer loop and why?
cards.back: The smaller table. The inner table is fully re-scanned once per outer block, so fewer outer blocks (⌈P(outer)/B⌉) means fewer expensive rescans of the big table.

cards.front: What kind of join predicates can ONLY block nested loop join handle (among the three join algorithms)?
cards.back: Non-equality predicates: similarity (distance(a,b) < 0.2), ranges (BETWEEN), and complex compound conditions. Hash and sort-merge joins require key equality to route or align matching rows.

cards.front: Hash Partition Join: the two phases and the best-case cost?
cards.back: Phase 1: hash both tables on the join key with the same function into matching partitions. Phase 2: for each partition pair, build a hash table on the smaller side in RAM and probe with the larger. Best case 3(N+M) + OUT — read, write partitions, read back.

cards.front: What is hash skew in HPJ and how is it fixed?
cards.back: A hot key (e.g. one user with 10M listens) overflows its partition past RAM while others fit. Fix: detect oversized partitions and recursively re-partition them with a different hash (or fall back to sort-merge), costing an extra pass on that data only.

cards.front: How does Sort-Merge Join work, in two phases?
cards.back: Phase 1: BigSort both tables on the join key. Phase 2: walk the two sorted runs with two pointers, advancing the smaller key and emitting all pairs whenever keys match. Output streams out already sorted on the join key.

cards.front: What is Sort-Merge Join's worst case?
cards.back: Heavy duplicate keys: a key with m matches on one side and n on the other emits an m × n cross-product, degenerating toward O(P(R) × P(S)) + OUT. OUT itself can dominate when match rates are high.

cards.front: Which join algorithm wins at small vs large buffer sizes, and why?
cards.back: Small B: HPJ — its ~3-pass cost is flat regardless of buffer. Large B: BNLJ — bigger blocks mean far fewer rescans of the inner table (2.6M IOs at B=10 down to 18K at B=10,000 in the course example). Pre-sorted input favors SMJ.

cards.front: How does an expensive write cost (high C_w) change which join algorithm wins?
cards.back: High C_w inflates SMJ (writes sorted runs) and HPJ (writes partition files) but leaves BNLJ untouched, since BNLJ only reads. High C_r scales all costs together and doesn't change the winner.
